232.title: How to be a guest
232.hook: seven weeks visiting seven doors, one first idea at a time, in each tradition's own words
232.howItsDone: Visitors to temples, gurdwaras, mosques, synagogues and churches usually learn the house customs first: shoes, head coverings, dress, silence, and asking before taking photographs.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed camp four with the reed and the emperor. Your line was longing and duty. Which plain duty did you do with a little longing in it? Day two hundred thirty-two, and camp five begins.

Think about the last time you were a guest at a friend's family dinner, a different family from yours. Maybe everyone paused before eating and you weren't sure whether to bow your head. Maybe there was a word everyone knew but you. Maybe you took your shoes off only after noticing everyone else's by the door. Being a good guest is a skill, and most of us learned it by accident. For the next seven weeks, we're going to be guests on purpose, visiting seven doors. Today, how to be a guest.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE'S FAMILY DINNER.` → `THE SHOES BY THE DOOR.` → `HOW TO BE A GUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the plan. Seven weeks, seven visits: Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, the Catholic tradition, Islam and Sikhism. Each is a whole door on this app, with years of its own lessons. We'll take one week in each, one first idea a day, the way someone at home in that tradition might first explain it to a friend. That's all it is: a visit. So, four house rules. First, use their words. Hindus say dharma, Jews say Torah, Muslims say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, Sikhs say Guru Nanak. We'll learn the words the way the family says them, not translate them into something more comfortable for us. Second, a visit is not a conversion and not a comparison. Nobody is being recruited, and nobody is being ranked. When we meet an idea that sounds like something from another door, we'll let each keep its own meaning, the way we kept Rumi and Marcus apart. Third, where a family disagrees with itself, we'll say so. Every tradition has schools and arguments, and we'll name who says what rather than pick a side. Fourth, don't pocket the silverware. It's easy to take a practice home, a candle, a chant, a bow, and strip away what it means. Try things if you like, as a guest, and remember whose table you're at. There's an old line from the Taittiriya Upanishad, a Hindu scripture, often recited in India: let the guest be as God to you. That's a host's duty. Our half of the bargain is to be worthy of it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide one way you'll be a good guest. Settle and breathe. Remember a time someone was a wonderful guest in your home, or a time you felt truly welcomed in someone else's. What did they do? Listen more than talk? Ask before touching things? Say thank you in the right way? Choose one thing you'll bring to these seven visits. Keep it simple. The bell holds the time.
How to be a guest. Use their words, don't convert or compare, name disagreements fairly, and don't pocket the silverware. Today's word.
screen: `HOW TO BE A GUEST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a guest, respectful. Today, in any space that isn't yours, an office, a friend's kitchen, a place of worship, notice the house rules before you act. Day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: Hinduism: dharma
233.hook: Hindus speak of dharma, the right order of things and the right way for each life
233.howItsDone: Many Hindus think of daily life in terms of dharma: duties to family, work, community and the gods, suited to one's stage of life, and many call their tradition Sanatana Dharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how to be a guest on seven visits. Your line was a guest, respectful. Did you notice someone's house rules before you acted? Day two hundred thirty-three, and our first visit: Hinduism.

Some mornings you know exactly what you're for. The kid needs breakfast, the shift starts at eight, the friend in the hospital needs a visit. Other mornings you look at ten possible lives on your phone, the travel one, the start-up one, the monk one, and feel you're failing at all of them. Hindus have a word that holds both of those mornings: the big order of the universe, and the small right way for this one life, today. For many Hindus it's so central that they call their whole tradition by it. Today's word: dharma.
screen: `SOME MORNINGS YOU KNOW.` → `TEN LIVES ON YOUR PHONE.` → `DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Dharma comes from a Sanskrit root, dhri, that means to hold, to support, to keep something standing. Dharma is what holds things up. In the widest sense it's the order of the cosmos: the sun rising, the seasons turning, the world held together rather than falling apart. In society it's what holds people together: justice, truthfulness, duty to family, care for guests and the poor. And in a single life it's the particular right way for you, at your stage of life, in your place. A student's dharma is to learn. A parent's is to raise children. A king's, in the old stories, is to protect. Many Hindus call their tradition Sanatana Dharma, the eternal dharma, because to them it isn't a set of beliefs so much as the way things truly hold together. Here's the famous line. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that it is better to do your own dharma, even imperfectly, than someone else's dharma well. Svadharma, your own dharma. Not the neighbor's path, however shiny. Honesty matters here. How far a person's dharma is set by their birth has been argued over by Hindus for centuries, and many Hindus today firmly reject tying it to caste. Other Indian traditions, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh, use the word dharma too, each in its own sense. This week, we're guests at a Hindu table. And for an ordinary Tuesday, the question dharma asks is simple: what holds things up, here, today, and what is mine to hold?
screen: `DHRI: TO HOLD, TO SUPPORT.` · `COSMOS, SOCIETY, ONE LIFE.` · `SANATANA DHARMA.` · `BETTER YOUR OWN, IMPERFECTLY.` · then, large: `MY OWN DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your duty for today. Settle and breathe. Think about your roles right now: child, parent, friend, worker, neighbor, student. Let one rise that needs you today. Then ask: what's the one thing, in that role, that would help hold things up? Not a whole life plan. Just today's piece. Name it plainly inside. The bell holds the time.
Dharma. From the Sanskrit for to hold: the order that holds the world up, and the right way for each life within it. Today's word.
Your line: my own dharma. Today, when someone else's path looks shinier, come back to the one thing that's yours to hold, and do it. Day two hundred thirty-three.

234.title: Hinduism: you are that
234.hook: a father dissolves salt in water to show his son the hidden essence: that is you (Chandogya Upanishad 6.13)
234.tomorrow: Hinduism: the act, not the fruit
234.howItsDone: Tat tvam asi is one of the great sayings of the Upanishads; Hindu students of Vedanta study it with a teacher, and the schools of Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva each explain it in their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharma, what holds the world up. Your line was my own dharma. What was yours to hold today? Day two hundred thirty-four.

A young man comes home after twelve years away at school. He's twenty-four, he's learned all the texts, and, the story says, he's a bit full of himself. His father, a teacher named Uddalaka, asks him one question: did you learn the thing by which everything else becomes known? The son, Shvetaketu, has no idea what he means. So his father starts teaching him again, from scratch, with ordinary things from the kitchen. A seed. Some honey. A river. And a lump of salt. Today's word: tat tvam asi.
screen: `HOME FROM SCHOOL, A BIT PROUD.` → `THE THING THAT MAKES ALL KNOWN.` → `A LUMP OF SALT.`

segments.voice: This is from the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the oldest Upanishads, the Hindu scriptures that explore the self and ultimate reality. Uddalaka tells his son: put this salt in a cup of water tonight, and bring it to me in the morning. In the morning he says, bring me the salt. The son looks. It's gone. Taste the water from the top, says his father. Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. The salt is everywhere in the water, though you can't see it anywhere. That, says Uddalaka, is how it is with the finest essence of all things, what the Upanishads call Brahman, ultimate reality. You don't see it, yet it's here, in everything. And then the line that the whole lesson has been circling. That is the real. That is the self. And then: tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu. The father says it again and again through this chapter, nine times in all. Tat, that. Tvam, you. Asi, are. Here's where honesty matters, because Hindu schools read these three words differently. Advaita Vedanta, following the teacher Shankara, reads it straight: your deepest self and Brahman are one and the same. The school of Ramanuja reads it as a close unity with a difference, the self belonging to Brahman the way a body belongs to its soul. The school of Madhva holds that the self and God are always distinct, and reads the line in a different way. All three are Hindu, and all three take the salt seriously. The father's picture holds: something invisible, in every drop.
screen: `A LUMP OF SALT, OVERNIGHT.` · `TOP, MIDDLE, BOTTOM: SALTY.` · `TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.` · `SHANKARA, RAMANUJA, MADHVA.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: taste a little salt water. If you have a glass of water and a pinch of salt, stir it in now. If not, just imagine it. Take a sip, slowly. Notice you can't see the salt, yet every sip carries it. Then close your eyes and breathe. Let the father's picture sit with you: something unseen, everywhere in the water. You don't need to decide what it means. The bell holds the time.
Tat tvam asi. You are that: the father's words after the salt, from the Chandogya Upanishad, read differently by different Hindu schools. Today's word.
Your line: you are that. Today, when you taste salt in your food, remember the cup of water and the invisible thing in every drop. Day two hundred thirty-four.

screen: `DAY 234 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HINDUISM: THE ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.`

235.title: Hinduism: the act, not the fruit
235.hook: Krishna tells Arjuna to act without clinging to results (Bhagavad Gita 2.47)
235.howItsDone: Many Hindus take karma yoga as a way of daily life: doing one's work and duties carefully, often offering them to God, without clinging to the results. Gita 2.47 is among its most quoted verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the father, the son and the salt: tat tvam asi. Your line was you are that. Did salt in your food remind you of the cup of water? Day two hundred thirty-five.

You send the job application, and then you check your email forty times. You post the thing, and then you watch the likes. You cook for someone, and then you study their face on the first bite. The work was done an hour ago, but your mind is still stuck on what comes back. The Bhagavad Gita, one of the best-loved Hindu scriptures, has a line about exactly this, spoken on a battlefield, to a man so frozen by consequences he can't lift his bow. Today's word: karma yoga.
screen: `CHECKING YOUR EMAIL FORTY TIMES.` → `A MAN WHO CAN'T LIFT HIS BOW.` → `KARMA YOGA.`

segments.voice: The Gita is set at the edge of a great battle in the epic Mahabharata. The warrior Arjuna looks across the field and sees his own cousins, teachers and elders on the other side. He drops his bow and says he won't fight. His charioteer is Krishna, whom Hindus revere as God come to earth. What follows is their conversation, seven hundred verses long. In chapter two, verse forty-seven, Krishna says, roughly: you have a right to your action, but never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting, and don't let that turn you toward doing nothing, either. That's karma yoga. Karma here means action, simply what you do. Yoga comes from a root meaning to yoke, to join: a discipline, a path. So karma yoga is the path of action, of doing your work fully while letting go of your grip on how it turns out. Notice what Krishna doesn't say. He doesn't say results don't matter, or that you shouldn't care. He says the doing is yours; the outcome isn't in your hands, so don't chain yourself to it. Many Hindus add that the work can be offered to God, done as worship. Hindus have read this battlefield in more than one way. Many take it as a real war and a warrior's real duty. Others, Mahatma Gandhi famously among them, read the battle as the struggle inside every person. Either way, the line lands on an ordinary Tuesday. Do the task. Do it well. Then open your hand.
screen: `ARJUNA DROPS HIS BOW.` · `A RIGHT TO THE ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.` · `KARMA, ACTION; YOGA, A PATH.` · `DO IT FULLY, THEN OPEN YOUR HAND.` · then, large: `THE ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one task to do, dropping the outcome. Settle and breathe. Pick one thing you'll do after this: an email, a meal, a conversation. Picture yourself doing it fully, with care, as well as you can. Now picture the moment it's done, and imagine opening your hand, palm up, and letting the result go wherever it goes. Try opening your actual hand now. The bell holds the time.
Karma yoga. The path of action: do your work fully, and let go of clinging to its fruits, as Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita. Today's word.
Your line: the act, not the fruit. Today, after you finish the task you chose, don't check on it for an hour. Let the doing be enough. Day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Hinduism: namaste
236.hook: the greeting bows to the divine in the other person
236.tomorrow: Hinduism: the lamp and the flower
236.howItsDone: Across India and Nepal, namaste or namaskar with palms joined is an everyday greeting and farewell, used with elders, guests and strangers, and it is also offered before images of the gods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma yoga, Krishna's advice to Arjuna on the battlefield. Your line was the act, not the fruit. Did you let a finished task go unchecked for an hour? Day two hundred thirty-six.

You've probably said it at the end of a yoga class, hands together, maybe feeling a little self-conscious. Or seen it on a T-shirt, a doormat, a coffee mug. It's become one of the most recognizable words from India anywhere in the world. But in Delhi or Kathmandu, it isn't a spiritual slogan. It's hello. It's what you say to your aunt, your neighbor, the shopkeeper, the guest at the door. And inside that everyday hello is something quite beautiful. Today's word: namaste.
screen: `THE END OF A YOGA CLASS.` → `IN DELHI, IT'S HELLO.` → `NAMASTE.`

segments.voice: Namaste is Sanskrit, and it's two small words joined. Namas means a bow, a bending, an act of honor. Te means to you. So namaste, word for word, is a bow to you. I bow to you. Usually it comes with a gesture: palms pressed together in front of the heart, fingers pointing up, and often a small bow of the head. The gesture itself has a name, anjali, which means an offering of joined hands. The same greeting is often said a little more formally as namaskar. Now, the phrase you may have heard, the divine in me bows to the divine in you. That's a popular explanation, especially in yoga studios, and it isn't in the word itself. But it isn't made up out of nothing, either. Many Hindus do explain the gesture this way: when you bow to another person, you're honoring the sacred present in them, the same reality we met two days ago in the salt and the water. So there are two honest layers. The literal one: I bow to you. The meaning many Hindus hear inside it: I honor what's holy in you. Either way, notice what the greeting does. It doesn't grab, it doesn't shake, it doesn't hug without asking. It lowers the head a little. It puts both hands where they can't hold anything. It makes a small space of respect between two people. A handshake says, I'm here. Namaste says, I see you, and I bow.
screen: `NAMAS: A BOW. TE: TO YOU.` · `PALMS TOGETHER AT THE HEART.` · `THE DIVINE IN YOU: A GLOSS.` · `A SMALL SPACE OF RESPECT.` · then, large: `I BOW TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet one person with care, starting now. Bring your palms together in front of your chest. Feel the two hands meet. Settle and breathe. Now picture someone you'll see today, even someone who irritates you a little. Picture their face. Lower your head slightly toward them, in your mind. Let the words be simply: I bow to you. Stay there, hands together. The bell holds the time.
Namaste. Sanskrit for a bow to you, with palms together at the heart; many Hindus hear in it an honor to the sacred in the other. Today's word.
Your line: I bow to you. Today, with the next person you greet, however you greet them, let a little of that bow be inside it. Day two hundred thirty-six.

237.title: Hinduism: the lamp and the flower
237.hook: daily worship at home often begins with a lamp and a flower
237.howItsDone: Many Hindu households keep a home shrine and perform a short daily puja: lighting a lamp and incense, offering flowers, water or food to the murti, sometimes with aarti and a prayer, before the day begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, namaste, palms together. Your line was I bow to you. Did a greeting today have a little bow inside it? Day two hundred thirty-seven.

Early morning in millions of Hindu homes, before the kettle, before the school run. In a corner of the kitchen, or a small cabinet, or a shelf in the living room, there's a little shrine: an image of a god, maybe Ganesha or Krishna or the goddess Lakshmi. Someone, often a grandmother or a mother, strikes a match, lights a small lamp, and sets down a fresh flower. Maybe a bell rings once. Maybe it takes two minutes. Then the day begins. Today's word: puja.
screen: `BEFORE THE KETTLE.` → `A SMALL SHRINE IN THE KITCHEN.` → `PUJA.`

segments.voice: Puja is the Sanskrit word for worship, honor, reverent attention. It can be grand, in a temple with priests, drums and hundreds of people, or tiny, one person at a home shrine before work. At its heart it's hospitality. The god is welcomed like an honored guest, and offered what you'd offer a guest: light, water, fragrance, flowers, food. The image in the shrine is called a murti, and many Hindus understand the deity as truly present in it during worship. A guest's note: murti is a better word than idol, which carries old insults. The lamp is often the first offering. A small clay or brass lamp, a diya, burning ghee or oil. In a ritual called aarti, the flame is waved in slow circles before the murti, then carried around, and people pass their hands over it and draw the warmth to their eyes and head. The food offered is afterward shared as prasad, a blessed gift. There's also darshan, which means seeing: to see the god, and to be seen. And the flower? The Bhagavad Gita has a lovely verse, chapter nine, verse twenty-six, where Krishna says that whoever offers him with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, he accepts it. The size of the gift doesn't matter. The love in it does. Hindu homes differ hugely: different gods, different families, different rules, and many Hindus don't keep a daily puja at all. But the shape of it is simple and very human: begin the day by offering light.
screen: `PUJA: WORSHIP AS HOSPITALITY.` · `THE MURTI, THE HONORED GUEST.` · `AARTI: THE FLAME IN CIRCLES.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · then, large: `ONE FLAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a lamp, set down a flower, or picture doing it. If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now. If you have a flower, a leaf or even a glass of water, set it beside the flame. If not, picture a small lamp in a quiet corner. Settle and breathe. Watch the flame. Let this be a small act of attention: something offered, not asked for. The bell holds the time.
Puja. Hindu worship, often at a home shrine: light, water, flowers and food offered to the god as to an honored guest. Today's word.
Your line: one flame. Tomorrow morning, before your phone, begin with one small act of attention: a candle, a window opened, a glass of water set down with care. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

238.title: Diwali, festival of lights
238.hook: the festival of lights, kept by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, each for their own reasons
238.tomorrow: Buddhism: the man under the tree
238.howItsDone: Hindu families light diyas, draw rangoli at the door, worship Lakshmi, share sweets and visit relatives; Sikhs light the Golden Temple for Bandi Chhor Divas; Jains mark Mahavira's liberation with lamps and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, puja, the lamp and the flower. Your line was one flame. Did you begin the morning with one small act of attention? Day two hundred thirty-eight, the last day of our Hindu visit.

Picture a whole city lit with tiny flames. Clay lamps lined along every windowsill, every rooftop, every doorstep. Colored powder patterns on the ground at the front door. Sweets carried house to house in boxes. Fireworks cracking over the rooftops until late. New clothes. Family on the phone from three continents. On the darkest night of the month, when there's no moon at all, hundreds of millions of people light lamps. Today we end our visit to Hinduism with its brightest festival. Diwali, the festival of lights.
screen: `A CITY LIT WITH TINY FLAMES.` → `THE DARKEST NIGHT, NO MOON.` → `DIWALI.`

segments.voice: Diwali comes from the Sanskrit Deepavali, a row of lamps. It usually falls in October or November, on a new moon night in autumn, which many Hindu calendars count in the month of Kartika, and in many places the celebration runs five days. But why light the lamps? Here's where being a good guest matters, because the answer depends on who you ask. For many Hindus, especially in north India, Diwali remembers the god Rama coming home to his city, Ayodhya, after fourteen years of exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana, and the people lighting lamps to welcome him. Many Hindus also worship the goddess Lakshmi that night, asking her blessing on home and work. In parts of south India, many remember Krishna's defeat of the demon Narakasura. In Bengal, the same night belongs to the goddess Kali. And it isn't only Hindu. Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release, remembering the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, freed from imprisonment in Gwalior Fort, and the Golden Temple in Amritsar blazes with lights. Jains remember the night Mahavira, their twenty-fourth great teacher, attained final liberation, and they light lamps because, as they tell it, the light of his wisdom had gone out of the world. Same night, same lamps, different stories. Each tradition keeps its own, and none needs the others' to make sense. What they share is the picture: light against the dark. And that closes our week with Hindus. Dharma. You are that. The act, not the fruit. Namaste. Puja. And now, a row of lamps.
